summary:
British Columbia stands under the national framework of Canada. No statute of the province restricts trans people's access to restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, to gender-affirming care, or to gender-related name use in schools, and the province has enacted no hostile legislation of its own in these areas.

British Columbia's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds across employment, housing, and public and private accommodations. Complaints against private businesses proceed under that statute, since Charter equality guarantees do not bind the private sector directly.

Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia. The Supreme Court of Canada has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality, and section 15 reaches all laws and government institutions in the province, including law enforcement authorities. Those guarantees remain subject to reasonable limits under section 1 and to the notwithstanding clause in section 33.

Vital statistics, including birth certificates and other identity documents, fall under British Columbia's provincial jurisdiction, so a gender-marker change on a provincial birth certificate is governed by the province rather than by Ottawa.
tangentialFactors:
British Columbia has no counterpart to the school and health restrictions adopted elsewhere in Canada. Saskatchewan's 2023 education amendment act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who request use of a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. Alberta's 2024 statutes covering health, education and sport faced legal challenges that were blocked when the provincial government passed a further statute amendment act in 2025 using the notwithstanding clause.

The national statistics agency reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in Canada in 2024, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% rise in 2023 over 2022, and 169% above the 2018 total. The national rate fell 2% to 11.9 per 100,000 population. Incidents targeting sexual orientation declined 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. These are national figures released on 30 March 2026 and they carry no provincial breakdown.

A national baseline score of 0.86 in the source's jurisdictional comparison rests on Charter equality protection, nationwide criminalisation of conversion therapy, and legal gender change available in every province including British Columbia.

A 2020 national public-opinion survey found that 87.6% of respondents said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person. The figure covers the country as a whole, is four years old at the time of the survey's publication, and says nothing about opinion within British Columbia specifically.
localsOnly:
Same-sex adoption has been legal in British Columbia since 1996, the first province in Canada to permit it, and British Columbia grants parental status to three or more intentional parents.

Residents seeking to change the gender marker on a birth certificate or another vital statistics record deal with the province's own vital statistics process, because those records sit under British Columbia's jurisdiction rather than a national one.
outOfScopeNotes:
The statistics agency release of 30 March 2026 covering 2024 police-reported hate crime reports national totals only. No British Columbia breakdown appears anywhere in the inventory, so the province's own hate-crime level is unresolved rather than established at any figure.

Egale Canada's 2024 analysis of police-reported hate-crime incidents affecting 2SLGBTQI people is a national report; the inventory records no British Columbia-level findings from it, and its provincial distribution is unresolved here.

The inventory documents no trans-specific killing or violence incident in British Columbia with a date and outcome, and no prevalence figure for the province is sourced. That is a gap in the sourcing, not evidence that no such incident has occurred.

The specific evidence, forms and waiting periods British Columbia requires for a gender-marker change on a birth certificate are not documented in the inventory. Only the province's jurisdiction over vital statistics is established; the procedure itself is unresolved.

No region-specific border, airport or security-screening practice affecting trans or gender-nonconforming travellers is documented in the inventory for British Columbia, and the inventory does not address any provincial use of the Charter's notwithstanding clause.
